MR. COATES-FAILURE OF MEMBER TO RISE FOR SINGING OF GOD SAVE THE QUEEN
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege affecting all members of this house. When a member takes a seat in this chamber at the beginning of a new parliament he must first swear an oath of allegiance to Her Majesty the Queen. The oath in question is to be found on page 406 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms and reads as follows:
I do swear that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II.
The words in the oath which I think are most significant are the words "faithful" and "allegiance". The most obvious definition of "faithful" is "loyal" and of "allegiance" either "loyalty" or "devotion". On Friday every member present in this house, with the exception of the member for Quebec West, stood and sang the prayer and anthem "God Save the Queen". We were displaying by our action our continued adherence to the oath we took on assuming our seats in this house; we were indicating our faithfulness and our true allegiance as members of parliament.
The member for Quebec West by his action indicated his unwillingness to stand by the oath to which he swore when he took his seat in this house and it is my belief that you, Mr. Speaker, or the committee on privileges and elections should determine whether he has any right to continue sitting in this chamber. This is not the first example of words or actions incompatible with the oath of allegiance, but it is certainly the most glaring and repulsive example to date in this twenty sixth parliament-

speakeroldname: Mr. H. A. Olson (Medicine Hat) moved:
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN ELEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That the eleventh report of the special committee on procedure and organization, presented to the house on October 7. 1964, be now concurred In.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving concurrence in the eleventh report on behalf of the committee on procedure and organization, I would like to make a few brief remarks respecting the four recommendations that are contained in it. If hon. members will refer to Votes and Proceedings of Wednesday, October 7, they will find the complete report. I might say that in that complete report there is a summary of some of the work that has been done by the committee in attempting to examine and make recommendations respecting the whole committee structure of the House of Commons. The committee on procedure and organization in fact appointed a subcommittee to address itself specifically to this problem, and to study and make recommendations respecting the committee structure of this house. I have before me several copies

Procedure Committee
of the summary that was prepared and the recommendations that are in the report. For the interest of the various parties perhaps they would like to have copies of this summary.
Generally speaking, Mr. Speaker, the subcommittee held a number of meetings to try to find ways and means of strengthening the committee structure of the House of Commons. One of the most important matters considered-and it is the main substance of this eleventh report-was that of giving committees the power to perhaps sit beyond prorogation, or at least to sit during an adjournment of the house. We looked into this matter in some detail with regard to the propriety of standing and special committees sitting after prorogation, and your subcommittee came to the conclusion that it was not competent to make recommendations with regard to sessions of standing or special committees after prorogation. If hon. members would refer to paragraph 14 of this report they will note that it says:
Your committee is of the opinion that the house should not empower a committee to sit beyond the prorogation of a session by simple resolution, or even by means of an amendment to standing order 65, since either course would infringe the royal prerogative. It appears to your committee that this reform could properly be implemented only by means of legislation. Ample precedent exists whereby the royal prerogative has been limited by means of an act of parliament, such legislation requiring the signification of the Queen's consent (not to be confused with the royal assent) prior to its final passage by the house. Since the practical exercise of the royal prerogative is today vested in Her Majesty's ministers, with whom the reality of power resides, your committee therefore recommends that the government give serious consideration to the introduction of such legislation at an early date.
The recommendation, therefore, is that the government should give consideration to this matter and introduce such legislation if they see fit. We believe it would be well for the government to consider this kind of action.
In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, we draw to the attention of the government and the house that there are two ways of dealing with this matter in the interim. One is that prorogation of a session could be delayed as long as possible to enable committees to meet while the house stood adjourned; and (b), where necessary a committee of the house could be constituted as a commission under the terms of the Inquiries Act, chapter 154 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, to enable it to continue its work beyond the prorogation of a session. Of these two alternatives your committee feels that the first sugges-

tion-that is, to delay prorogation-would be the most desirable.
I think it would be well for hon. members to consider the problems this house encountered last year when a number of committees were sitting and we were working toward a prorogation date of, I think it was, December 21. Many of those committees had insufficient time to complete their work, to report to the house and to move concurrence therein before prorogation. It is well known to all hon. members that all the work of a committee dies on prorogation unless a report is made to the house which is considered, adopted or concurred in by the house.
This session we see the possibility of two of our standing committees of this house requiring time beyond what may be considered an appropriate date for prorogation. One of those committees is the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines which is considering Bill No. C-120; the other is the standing committee on agriculture and colonization which is considering the matter of feed grains for eastern Canada. Perhaps both these committees would need to sit beyond the date when most of the other business of the house has been completed.
We do not believe it ought to be automatic that these standing or special committees sit when the house is not in session, but we do think that by adjourning rather than proroguing and passing a simple resolution or motion in the house, certain of these committees could sit beyond the adjournment date.
The third recommendation, Mr. Speaker, deals with the matter of continuing the membership of committees from one session to another. We think standing order No. 65 should be amended by the substitution in line 2 of the words "the first session of each parliament" for the words "each session". That would enable the membership of committees to be named for the duration of a parliament instead of for the duration of a session.
This becomes important, Mr. Speaker, because if we look back in the records of this session of the twenty sixth parliament we find that while the striking committee was set up on the first day of the session, as required under our standing orders, it was not until March 11, as reported at page 777 of Hansard, that the Prime Minister moved the motion that would set up the standing committees of this house. We believe the reason this action was taken even as early as March 11, which was nearly 30 days after the house

was in session, was that it was necessary to get the external affairs committee functioning to deal with a specific matter.
We also note, Mr. Speaker, that only one standing committee was set up on that date, and that it was not until April 10, as recorded at page 1989 of Hansard, that the chief government whip was in a position to make the motion naming the membership of all of the standing committees of the House of Commons. So you can see, Mr. Speaker, that nearly two months had gone by after the commencement of the session before these committees were actually in existence; for certainly it cannot be argued that they were in existence before names of members were attached to them.
We believe that if this recommendation to amend standing order 65 were accepted by the house and by the government, and the motion was moved to set up these committees at the beginning of a parliament rather than at the beginning of each session, then the first day of each session when parliament gets under way the committees would be in existence and the membership would be named. In this event there would be no waiting for the various parties to supply names each session for the different committees.
The fourth recommendation, Mr. Speaker, deals with the terms of reference. We believe that a committee's terms of reference, particularly a standing committee, should automatically include the power to appoint subcommittees. The motion relating to the powers of standing committees should in the future be moved, we think, in the following terms. First of all, this was the motion moved by the Prime Minister, as appears at page 777 of Hansard:
That the standing committees of this house be severally empowered to examine and inquire into all such matters and things as may be referred to them by the house; and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, with power to send for persons, papers and records.
Our recommendation is that these words be included:
-and to delegate to subcommittees all or any of their powers except the power to report direct to the house.
It appeared that even during this session it would have been expedient for at least one or two committees to have the power to set up subcommittees, and I refer specifically again to Bill C-120, which deals with three separate areas of railway transport matters in Canada. It seems to me that it would be well for the house to delegate this power
Procedure Committee
to that committee so that three separate studies could be carried on at the same time.
It will be recognized that these recommendations being made today by your committee must be the subject of action on the part of the government so that effect can be given to them. While concurrence today would not necessarily mean that these recommendations would automatically be put into effect, it would give to the government an indication that we believe the things we suggest should be done. Therefore, on behalf of the committee, I recommend to hon. members of this house that this report be concurred in, giving an indication that they think these recommendations are desirable.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that in so far as a complete study of recommendations respecting the committee structure of the house is concerned, this eleventh report must be considered as an interim report. Your committee is continuing to study this matter and will be coming forward at a later date with other recommendations as to committee size, function and vested authority. It is the opinion of the committee on procedure and organization that these matters we are now recommending for consideration today require immediate attention for the business of this particular session.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN ELEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as seconder of this motion I am pleased to join with the hon. member for Medicine Hat in asking for the concurrence of the house in the eleventh report of the special committee on procedure and organization. I hope all hon. members have read this report which can be found in Votes and Proceedings of October 7 last; because it outlines not only the three immediate proposals we are recommending to the government, but also some of the problem areas in this whole field of committees which the committee on procedure and organization, through its subcommittee on committees, is planning to undertake and study.
I think it is accurate to say that all hon. members of that committee, and I hope all hon. members of this house, feel there is a great deal to be done to both rationalize and strengthen the committee system of this house, not only to make the committees themselves more effective but also indeed to make the house itself more effective. It seems to me that if we have a stronger, more rational and more effective committee system we will be able to cover a great deal more ground in our committees and accomplish much more by

Procedure Committee
way of tightening debate in this chamber. The two seem to me to go hand in hand.
For all these reasons I hope all hon. mem-bets will again read this whole report, since it does outline some of the areas we plan to study. I know the members of the committee will be grateful for suggestions from hon. members as to what other areas they think we might look into.
Our immediate request is for concurrence in essentially three recommendations. One is that the government give consideration at some time to introducing legislation which will make it possible permanently for committees to continue from one session to another within a parliament. As has already been said, this will involve some limitation on the royal prerogative; therefore the Queen's consent will have to be secured before this legislation is introduced. The committee felt, however, that this was the appropriate way of going about it, and we hope that at some time the government will make it possible for committees to sit between sessions within a parliament, as a routine or automatic thing. In the meantime, until that is done, we suggest either of two courses of action, and particularly favour the course of action which would allow committees to continue sitting by, in effect, postponing prorogation as was done during the war, I believe, until the day before a new session begins.
As the hon. member for Medicine Hat has said, our second proposal is to make it possible for the membership of committees to be named for an entire parliament. I am sure there should not be any disagreement with that.
The next proposal is to allow committees to appoint subcommittees. This latter recommendation will be particularly important if in the reorganization of the committee structure of this house we should decide that it would be preferable to have fairly large committees covering broad fields of action, functional areas as they are called, rather than a large number of very small committees. If we have fairly large ones it will be absolutely essential that they be enabled to appoint subcommittees.
Beyond this immediate report we hope to go into the whole question of what powers committees should have. For example, should committees have the power to initiate? Should committees discuss estimates as well as legislation in their appropriate fields? Should there be new committees to which we have not given any thought at all in this house, as for instance a committee on statutory in-

struments or delegated legislation such as they have in the United Kingdom? Should there be only standing committees and should all the work be done by these, through subcommittees, or will we still require the occasional special committee? How many members should be on each committee or on each subcommittee? Most important, what powers should committees have? It seems to me this will be by far the most crucial problem we will be discussing. No doubt there will be further reports brought to this house.
I think we are all aware of the fact that we do operate under a system of responsible cabinet government. We have not thought of creating a series of small cabinets within the House of Commons in rivalry to the cabinet itself. There could be no thought, therefore, of copying the United States system, as has been suggested, ynless we change our whole system of government, which we are not thinking of doing, at any rate in this committee. However, within the confines of the system of responsible cabinet government surely it is possible to give larger functions and stronger and clearer powers-I would hope even the power of initiation-to our standing committees of this house. As I say, this will come up in the future. It is not something for which we are asking concurrence today; it is something for the future. It is something that, if the recommendations we are making today are concurred in, will be easier for the committee to discuss.
Nor is there any reason why we should limit our discussion to these problem areas mentioned in this report. There are other suggestions that might be made, and I hope that in the course of the next few months as this committee continues its work, hon. members will be bringing forward other suggestions as to ways in which the committee system, and parliament itself through its committee system, can be strengthened.
For example, I have always felt that there are some bills which could be referred to committees after first reading. This is quite contrary to the general practice under our parliamentary system where the principle is always decided upon before the bill goes to committee. There are occasions, particularly when our parliamentary timetable is so crowded, upon which we could send non-controversial, non-partisan bills to a committee after first reading, provided the committees themselves were representative and that there would be a full discussion there of this type

of bill. There are bills right now on the order paper which I believe could be referred to a committee.
This is one kind of suggestion which is not made here and to which I think we could give some serious consideration. I urge all hon. members to try to stretch their imaginations a little on the use of the committee system of this house to see if they cannot come up with something that will be compatible with the system we have of responsible cabinet government, and at the same time compatible with the needs of the kind of complex system in which we live today.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN ELEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words with respect to the motion for concurrence in this eleventh report. I do so both as a member of the committee and on behalf of this party.
The adoption of this motion, Mr. Speaker, does not have the precise effect that the adoption of some other motions for concurrence in reports of Your Honour's committee have had. The adoption does not actually effect any change. Nevertheless, we as members of the committee feel that this is a very important report we are presenting to the house, and that the heart of it is something very significant. The heart of it, as we see it, is that the house should give consideration to the greater use of committees.
I agree with the position just stated both by the hon. member for Medicine Hat and the hon. member for Northumberland. We are not trying to change our system of government, but we do feel the house could benefit from a strengthening of its committees and from a greater use of them. As we see it, there are two things that are necessary if this is going to be done and in this instance both these things fall on the shoulders of the government.
In the first place, we have to do something about the royal prerogative that makes it necessary for us to re-establish committees at every session, and consequently prevents committees meeting between sessions. By the terms of the royal prerogative a session of parliament starts when we are called into session by the crown, and it ends with prorogation. Between prorogation and the next summoning of a session of parliament, there is nothing that parliament or its committees can do. This can be resolved by legislation affecting the royal prerogative and, as a committee, we are asking the house to ask the government to give serious study to this
Questions
matter and take action upon it at an early date.
Another step that will be necessary if we are going to strengthen committees and use them more will be for the government to take a positive position and ask the house to refer more matters to committees so they can be studied thoroughly, and so that good use of the committees and of the members of those committees can be made. All of us feel, and I think the feeling is generally shared by the members of our committee on committees, that there should be certain times of the year when the house itself need not be in session but when the committees might be able to meet and deal on a full time basis with matters referred to them.
Without going into detail, which certainly is not necessary at this time, I join with the other two members who have spoken in saying that our studies have convinced us that a very much greater use can be made of committees. In this report all we are saying is that we hope the government will take the necessary steps to see that what is requested in this report is implemented at an early date.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATUS OF QUEBEC DELEGATION IN PARIS
speechtext: No, the Canadian government has not asked the government of France to grant diplomatic status to the Quebec delegation in Paris. For that matter, the government of Quebec has never at any time asked that its delegation in Paris be given diplomatic status. The government of Canada has therefore asked on several occasions, and in complete agreement with the government of Quebec, privileges and immunities for the Quebec delegation in Paris comparable to those which have been accorded for a long time by the British government to the agent general of Quebec and to other provincial representatives in London. Our discussions with the authorities of the government of France on this subject continue, especially through the intervention of our ambassador in Paris. I hope that the government of France will soon be in a position to grant to the Quebec delegation, and in due course to any other delegation of a province of Canada which might be established in Paris, appropriate privileges and immunities which would facilitate the effective accomplishment of their tasks.

Mr. Speaker, while I have the floor I should like to reply to a question directed to me by the right hon. leader of the official opposition last Friday, which appears at the bottom of page 9116 of the English version of Hansard of October 16, 1964. I shall quote the exact text in the language in which it was asked as this is always the best way to proceed. I quote:

I should like to ask the Minister of Justice whether in the course of an interview on the C.B.C. yesterday, dealing in particular with the formula for the amendment of the constitution, he was asked a question to this effect: "Does this formula mean that the door is now open for an associate state?" And did he reply thereto in approximately these words: "You might put it that way"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT BY JUSTICE MINISTER RESPECTING RADIO INTERVIEW
speechtext:
The answer is no, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, I have now obtained a transscript of the question as put to me and the answer I gave, and I wish now to read it into the record as being my answer to the question.

Q.-If, for instance, it should happen at a given moment that four provinces, if not more, decide to delegate important powers to the federal government in years to come and that the province of Quebec, for reasons of her own which we can all

Inquiries of the Ministry understand, should decide to keep such jurisdictional powers would it not be possible to arrive at some sort of associate state status for the two ethnic groups, the two nations?

Up to a point, it would be possible. The reason is that in at least four important sectors-for instance, the one dealing with civil rights and property, which the province of Quebec looks upon as something sacred-well, we could have a delegation of authority to the Canadian parliament by seven, eight or nine provinces and then, of course, for that purpose, well, there could exist between Quebec and the other provinces, let us say a difference, if not in actual status-for the constitution would remain the same-at least a difference in fact.

Those are the tacts, and this is the record.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words with respect to clause 2. I propose to move an amendment to this clause, but let me say it is only the first of two or three amendments which we may wish to move to this clause. As you are aware, sir, we are now operating under a rule which gets us right down to business; therefore I shall come straight to the point concerning which I wish to move an amendment.
Clause 2 paragraph (f) lists a certain number of general holidays. The objective which the minister announced with respect to this proposed code was that we in this parliament should fix by law certain basic and reasonable standards. Not to do so would be to defeat his own purpose. The minister appeared extremely uncomfortable as he sought to oppose the amendment which was put forward by hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre. He surely will not argue that the addition of one holiday falling in a month distinct from those in which the other listed holidays occur would raise the minimum standards in this country so high that the balanced package, if that is what he considers this proposed code to be, would be seriously upset. I think it is foolish when we are considering an important piece of legislation such as the bill before us to create a situation which will result in arguments brought forward in the house from time to time in the years which lie ahead. Surely the minister, if he expects

Canada Labour Code
to remain in his present portfolio for any appreciable length of time, cannot relish the prospect of having to face, as undoubtedly he will have to do unless the amendment is adopted, the introduction of bills by private members of this house, probably by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, next year and the year after that and in all the years following seeking to incorporate into this labour code this one extra statutory holiday. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to speak in support of the proposed amendment. While I am speaking the Minister of Labour might take the opportunity of conferring on this particular point with his experienced colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs; he might tell the hon. gentleman what we are discussing and see what he has to say about it. I say this because the Secretary of State for External Affairs has had a good many years of experience in the House of Commons and realizes, as the present Minister of Labour does not realize, that there are occasions when a government should accept suggestions which come forward from the opposition benches, and yield without losing face.
The Minister of Labour is using the same method as was adopted by the Minister of Agriculture a few days ago-refusing to accept any suggestions from this side of the house, as a result of which a prolonged debate developed. Here you have a reasonable suggestion put forward from the opposition side to include one more holiday in the list of statutory holidays; and of all days that should be suggested, it is Remembrance day. A government that was not completely insensitive to the feelings of the people of this country would accept that amendment,

apologize for the error of omission, and we would get on with the rest of the bill.
Over the years the Royal Canadian Legion, army and navy veterans, and other veterans organizations, have suggested that Remembrance day should be observed as a holiday, and observed not simply for a day off from work or from the troubles that beset us month by month but a day of actual remembrance of the sacrifices made in warfare. I think it is high time that the parliament of Canada recognized this day for what it is, a day in which the people of this country and the leaders of the country as represented by the various governments, dominion and provincial, take note of the fact that our freedom has been preserved by the sacrifices of Canadians in the past. That is what Remembrance day is.
During the time that I had the privilege of serving as minister of veterans affairs I examined with the officials of that department this problem of the observance of Remembrance day, and I raised this point with them, pointing out that I had observed that there had been a tendency to let the importance of this day slip a little bit as the years go by. It happened between the two world wars. I know from my experience then, when I was engaged in the field of education, that the tendency in many areas was to let the school children and teachers observe Remembrance day, whereas the adults should have been the ones who were setting the example. In some areas that was changed. Then we had the second world war. Remembrance day means even more now than it did in between the two world wars. So I discussed this problem with the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs and said, "We must do something to assist the serious people in this country who want to properly observe Remembrance day". As a result of some of those discussions we had produced by the national film board the film "The Fields of Sacrifice", which was shown last year for the first time and is now available for all communities across Canada in the 16 millimetre version. This was a government response to the observance of Remembrance day. I had some other ideas with regard to that day, which I was not able to bring into effect due to various changes that took place.
However, here we have the opportunity now presented to us for government recognition, recognition by parliament, of the importance of Remembrance day by adding it to the list of statutory holidays. Amongst these other holidays it ranks very high in the list.

As has already been mentioned, Mr. Chairman, one or two of the days mentioned in this bill cannot conceivably be raised to the level of Remembrance day when it is properly considered. I suggest this government should really consider this matter seriously now, pause for reflection if you wish, and take this matter under consideration; but I would think even better still would be to accept immediately the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and supported by people on this side of the house. This is a day that should be recognized as a statutory holiday, and if it becomes a statutory holiday the adult population of this country can set the proper example to our young people as to what this day means. As it is now, it is a school holiday and school children will recognize it as they do any other holiday. But this should be a day of dedication on the part of the adult population of this country, which understands the sacrifices involved in warfare, on which to express our hope that we will not be involved in war again; that the younger generation will not in their turn have to go through the holocaust of a great war. This is the purpose, as I see it, of Remembrance day. We should make this day available to veterans and the friends and relatives of veterans so they may solemnly observe this day as it should be observed. Mr. Chairman, those are some of the reasons why we feel this amendment should be accepted immediately by the government.

It is for this reason that I am going to support the amendment proposed.
Another point that has been ignored by the hon. member for Essex West is this. There is a slight difference in the degree of local autonomy between the Yukon government and the government of the Northwest Territories. The Yukon government is an entirely elected body and in many spheres of operation is completely autonomous. Unhappily, the government of the Northwest Territories has not proceeded nearly so far in the direction of self-government as has the government of the Yukon. At the time the previous administration left office we had launched a program that was designed to accelerate the movement of the government of the Northwest Territories toward a greater degree of decentralization. I was the responsible minister for some three years, and it did not require a very long period of time to realize that the Northwest Territories, and to a lesser extent the Yukon Territory, would never come into its own until it had a greater degree of local responsibility and initiative.
We were carrying on negotiations with the labour organizations that are active in these territories with a view to encouraging the governments of the respective territories to establish a labour code of their own. According to this legislation before us it would seem that no further progress has been made in these conversations and discussions. I was quite disappointed in this, along with the hon. member for Northwest Territories, who above all members of this house knows whereof he speaks because he was a part of the administration of the Northwest Terri-
Canada Labour Code
tories for a number of years and made an outstanding contribution in that regard before he became the elected representative of the people there.
I was surprised to see that the present government, when bringing this bill before the house, had decided it was going to continue the discriminatory approach to the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories which has existed far too long for the good of the general development-the political development as well as the economic development- of these territories. I think that if the amendment is accepted by the committee it will serve as a catalytic agent, particularly in the Yukon where the government, I am sure, is ready to deal with the matter of establishing a labour code of its own. It will certainly act as a catalytic agent in getting moving once again the efforts that were under way to give a greater degree of self-government to the Northwest Territories. There has been a complete stalemate in this development. We had the matter before the committee on mines, forests and waters for several weeks, but the committee died a premature death. I think that here is an excellent opportunity for this committee, by expressing its opinion on this amendment, to give a prod to the powers that be to get in motion once again this movement toward self-government and local autonomy.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether, before the question is put, the minister could state to the committee his position on a matter that relates precisely to this kind of problem. I have asked him on repeated occasions whether there is any possibility of the staff of his department looking into this and related kinds of labour problems within the northern territories, with a view to assessing the present situation. I am not prepared to accept the statement of hon. members that this would work a hardship on someone in the Northwest Territories. I do not know out of which part of the atmosphere they draw this conclusion, or on what advice. The minister has not told me who advised him that this would work a hardship. Was it the officials of the department of northern affairs who said it would, or is it just because of some feeling that the territorial council would do something along this line?
The point I am making which has application to the amendment before the committee is this. Not nearly enough research and examination has gone into this kind of exclusion. I for one am not prepared to admit that it is in the best interests of the northern territories to make this exclusion or that it will afford some sort of protection which the business community in the Canadian north needs. That is always the argument which is used whenever an effort of social reform is brought down-that it is not in the best interests of those it will affect to have this sort of help. The minister has a division which does this sort of thing and I asked him about this the last time his estimates came up. I do not want the officials of the department of northern affairs brought in because already they have too much to do

in the Northwest Territories and have their fingers in too many pots in the Canadian north. But it is time this was curbed, and curbed smartly.
To get back to the purport of the clause, what guarantee has this committee that the minister and his officials will give the territorial council the sort of advice which is required? The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona pointed out that right now the council of the Northwest Territories is made up of nine people. Four of these people are elected from some part of the north and five are appointed. The five who are appointed live in southern Canada. They are appointed by the governor in council. In at least two cases they are also federal civil servants who give advice to the officials of the department of northern affairs. Here is the kind of inbred problem, if you will, that we face now.
I am not reassured when the minister says they have done nothing about this in all these years, but he thinks they are going to do something and because of that the government does not want to step on their toes. Surely the minister can say what studies were undertaken and on what basis he excluded the territories. It is not enough just to say that it seemed like a good idea at the time. I want to know who advised him in this regard; and second, can he tell the committee what sort of advice will be presented to the council? The minister said the council of the Northwest Territories will be considering a document which will offer advice about these matters and whether or not it will be hurtful to certain business enterprises in the territories to implement a standards code. I do not think we should have two labour standards codes in this country any more than I think we should have two flags. We are getting too many instances where there is one thing for one part of the country and another thing for another part of the country. I am still not convinced that northern workers need less protection than southern workers.
I am aware of the observations made by the hon. member for Essex West-and there was probably a moral in this, namely that people who live that far south should not advise people who live in the north, and vice versa. I have yet to make a speech on labour conditions in the city of Windsor, and I doubt that I will. None the less I wish the minister would give the committee some information as to the quality of the advice

Canada Labour Code
that is going to be given to the federal authority prior to the next meeting of the Northwest Territories council. That would not be betraying any secrets. I for one am not prepared to tell our northerners not to worry, that the department of northern affairs officials love them and will look after their best interests, and that they need no guarantees of any kind. That sort of nonsense has pervaded too much of our legislation. Surely the minister can tell the committee what advice is being given the council of the Northwest Territories, and who it was advised his department to exclude the Northwest Territories and the Yukon from the provisions of this bill.

Mr. Chairman, I think this amendment is very worth while. I am wondering whether the minister will give some consideration to a charge which has been made this afternoon, namely that the former minister of northern affairs found himself in the same position as the present minister has now been advised to take. Does this not flow from the fact that the same advisers who made this decision before are making the decision now?
I have several persons from the Northwest Territories who live in my constituency who have had occasion to write to me concerning compensation, vacation pay, and so on. In two cases I went from the council to the Department of Labour, and then to the department of northern affairs and the Department of Public Works. In each case we came across a decision which had been made by the director of industrial relations in the department, which I think was wrong. I also think this official was wrong in advising the former minister of northern affairs, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, and is wrong today in advising the present minister.
Clause 3 (h) makes reference to any work which is before or after its execution declared by parliament to be to the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces. This is a highly technical clause which has disallowed the benefits of labour relations legislation to persons working in the Northwest Territories and, I presume, the Yukon. If we are to write into this bill an exclusion of the Yukon and Northwest Territories we will not be meeting the requirements which the Minister of Labour has declared must be met. Because of the direction being given and the vast amount of legalistic confusion which exists through the actions of five or six agencies having relatively equal responsibilities in the territories, we are not well advised here, and the minister is not well advised to put himself in the position of making an exception of a very large segment of the country in regard to industries in those areas over which he has jurisdiction.
I think the minister should think again about this matter because he is recommending an exclusion which must indicate that he had knowledge that such a thing has worked to the disadvantage of workers in that area. I thought some time ago that this bill should apply mainly to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon because this is one place in which the federal government can give leadership, and I congratulate the minister for this. However, I do not think this exemption should be left in the bill in the form it is, although he may be perfectly right that there are segments of the labour field in Northwest Territories and the Yukon in which it would be difficult to implement the terms of this bill. This means there is no difference between the application of this exemption in one part of Canada compared with the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
I think the minister is being unfair to himself and is not giving the leadership he wants to give by exempting for one reason or another a small segment of the country to which this measure would bring a great deal of benefit. I am sure other hon. members have also brought before the minister cases which would be effected by clause 3 (h) to which I have referred. Normally even work done by the federal government is not classified as being in the interest of Canada or Canadians, as it reads in this bill, which means that there must be a special declaration to this effect. If we allow this exception we will be providing a loophole in respect of this problem which has developed over the years, and which has been discussed and argued with the officials of the department on numerous occasions; and it will continue to exist. If the minister is not prepared to support the amendment now before us, I think he might find it to his advantage to reconsider it, in terms of those works being done by the federal government in the Northwest Territories which are not specifically declared by the governor in council, or by the parliament of Canada as being to the general advantage of Canada. If the minister is not prepared to support this amendment I hope that he will indicate he is prepared to propose an amendment which is perhaps not as all-embracing as the one now before us.

In this event a contractor who may be bound by his contract to carry mail for anything up to four years will suddenly find that he has to pay his drivers $1.25 an hour, with the average rural route run taking 20220-583

three or four hours. That is $6 or more per day. I think this is another instance where the bill in respect of a minimum wage cannot be applied, and I point this out for this reason. -any work or undertaking that, although wholly situated within a province, is before or after its execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces, and-
What is meant by the phrase "to be for the general advantage of Canada"?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: This is also a standard paragraph or section in all our labour statutes. The parliament of Canada is free to declare a work to be to the general advantage, and if such a work is done it comes within federal jurisdiction. For instance, uranium mining has been declared to be to the general advantage of Canada and is under federal jurisdiction. The wheat elevators, flour and cereal mills have also been declared by parliament to be to the general advantage of Canada, and for that reason come under federal jurisdiction.

speechtext:
I would refer the minister to section 174 of the Canada Grain Act which says:
All elevators in Canada heretofore or hereafter constructed are hereby declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada.
I am wondering how this clause would apply to the managers of these elevators in the fall, when the farmers are taking their crops off and when they get into the elevators at all times of night. Clause 3(3) of this bill says:
This act does not apply to or in respect of employees who are
(a) managers or superintendents or who exercise management functions,
Would this apply to all elevator operators on the prairies in the fall months when the crops are coming off? They certainly could not work a 40 hour week and take in all the crops.

speechtext:

In the operations of the country elevators there are peak periods, and these peak periods go beyond the standard hours of work for a day or a week, and this might be regarded as an excessive burden on the elevators with respect to overtime.
The officials of my department have had discussions with representatives of the elevators, and we expect that the application of another clause in the bill, providing for the averaging of the standard hours beyond a period of two weeks, would take into account the problems raised by country elevators with respect to the application of hours.

speechtext: In the case of the country elevators I wonder if this should not be spelled out in definite terms so that it would not come up as a point of argument at a later date. subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I think it would be unfortunate to exclude the country elevators specifically from the total operations of the
Canada Labour Code
bill, because we want to apply its principles to the employees of federal undertakings, including country elevators. We think it is reasonable to provide for an averaging over a period greater than two weeks and, if need be, this could be extended over a period of a year, which would provide an opportunity to level off the seasonal peaks with the seasonal valleys. This is one protection in the bill that I think will go a long way to meet the difficulties.
When we come to the transitional provisions I shall have something to say in connection with the opportunities available for a deferment, where the application of the hours might be prejudicial to the employees or to the operation of an undertaking under this bill. There are two protections here that will look after the situation without spelling it out specifically, because I think it would be unfortunate to exclude these people.

speechtext: First of all, there is a feeling, presumably that these are managers, though they have entered into a collective agreement as employees of the wheat board in a Saskatchewan trade union

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I wish to support the minister by saying I certainly think all grain elevator operators should come under this legislation because they are in a group which is not covered by provincial labour legislation and they should have the benefit of this bill, particularly as far as statutory holidays, vacations with pay and so on are concerned-the minimum wage provision scarcely affects them because most of them are paid well in excess of it.
However, I am sure the minister is aware there are some problems. The key problem is

Canada Labour Code
that there are times of the year when the quotas are open and when farmers must be able to deliver their grain. At such times the elevator operators must be there. On the other hand there are long periods in the winter, and when quotas are not open, when the job is merely a caretaking proposition with occasional cleaning of grain and so on. I think the minister could work this problem out under subclause 2 of clause 5 and under the regulations which provide for averaging. We encountered the same difficulty with respect to oil drillers under provincial legislation, but in the end agreement was reached between the employers and the employees under which for certain months in the year the employees worked on the basis of a 30 hour week while in another season of the year they worked on a 48 hour basis. It averaged out. If extra hours had to be worked, then of course overtime was paid.
I think a solution could be worked out in this case. I should like to ask the minister whether he is satisfied that he has the necessary powers under the regulatory provisions to enable him to deal with the situation in this way. I agree it is essential that the elevators should be kept open and that someone should be there whenever grain is delivered. This particularly applies during the fall when grain is wet and has to be delivered to the elevator and dried. This might mean working 12 to 16 hours a day. It would, of course, be unfortunate if we tried to impose an eight hour day at that time of the year and then stuck to an eight hour day in the winter when there is less work to be done. I hope the minister is satisfied he has the necessary powers, after consultation with the grain operators, because I believe that by making the necessary adjustments in the regulations he could solve this problem. The operators must be covered by the legislation, yet the legislation must at the same time provide sufficient flexibility to enable farmers to deliver their grain to the elevators at any reasonable time.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: May I suggest that this clause stand until we have an opportunity to ascertain what subclause (5) means? It would give us an opportunity to look up the grain act and make sure that the western producers are protected.

speechtext:
I am content that it be allowed to stand and I am satisfied we can meet this problem.
Clause stands.

speechtext:

Nothing in this act authorizes the doing of any work on Sunday that is prohibited by law.

Clause agreed to.

Standard hours of work.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: I think this is the proper place to ask the minister whether he can now give an explanation of the problems I raised when we were discussing this question last week in connection with groups of workers such as railway workers and others. The illustration I used last week was the case of sleeping car, dining car and parlour car employees who are now working substantially more than a 48 hour week. If they were included in the provisions of this measure and if the railway company reduced their hours of work to 48 while holding them to the hourly rate established by the contract, they would suffer a very severe reduction in pay.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I think the place to deal with this is under clause 51. Presumably we are already agreed on the principle of the eight hour day and the 40 hour week, and clause 51 gives us an opportunity, as it were, to time the application of this principle, taking into account considerations of the kind mentioned by the hon. member. I think if we could defer consideration of this matter and others like it

there are a number of them -until we come to clause 51 we would have a better discussion. Presumably we would do nothing at this point to upset the acceptance of the principle on second reading.

speechtext:

negotiate a new contract, but those negotiations could conceivably lead to a substantial reduction in take home pay at the end of the month.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: That is the problem we are attempting to deal with in the clause I have just mentioned. I think it would make for a better discussion if we were to postpone this issue unil we reach that particular clause. It would give us a chance, too, to deal with some other aspects. The case of the country elevators is really the same type of problem.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am sure that my hon. friend, along with the rest of us, will not mind having the discussion on clause 51 rather than on clause 5, provided we are not precluded from putting forward the proper amendment necessary to the appropriate clause. Things are going fairly well today so we thought this might be the proper time to move another amendment.
Clause 51 as we understand it merely provides for the 18 months transitional period. The minister has not yet accepted the idea of writing such a provision into the legislation. But if he were to accept it as the result of discussion in this chamber, to which clause would these words be added; would they be added to clause 5, or to clause 51?

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would not raise a point of order if my hon. friend proposed an amendment to clause 51 to cover that point.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: All I can say to the minister is, many thanks for the invitation. We do not need it, but we will accept it.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the minister at this point a question regarding the matter raised by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek and the hon. member for Assiniboia. Looking at clause 5 (2), the last few words are:
-in such manner and in such circumstances as may be prescribed by the regulations, as an average for a period of two or more weeks.
If that is the case, I am wondering whether this gives the minister sufficient flexibility to deal with the problem raised by hon. members regarding grain elevators on the prairies.
Canada Labour Code

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: This would permit us to arrive at an average for a period of two or more weeks. We would have the authority to average over a full year, if that were necessary. Presumably the premium paid would apply only beyond 2,000 hours, because on a yearly average the total hours permissible within the 40 hour week would be 2,000 and beyond that overtime would apply. Presumably this would meet the seasonal character and would also preserve the principle of the 40 hour week. This certainly goes a long way in levelling off, I would think.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Then the minister is satisfied that this is flexible enough to meet the problem outlined?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: I am satisfied that it is sufficiently flexible, based on the conversations we have had. But it may be that clause 51 is another place where this situation could also be helped.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister is correct with regard to clause 5(2), but one of the points that I think could be raised as an eventual argument is that the elevator operator might possibly go to the elevator at eight o'clock in the morning and be there until six o'clock at night. So far as he is concerned, he can say he is on duty full time, and I do not think the two weeks would be enough extra time to cover the extra hours he would be there for that period of time. This is the part I am concerned about. Possibly the elevator operator is not buying grain for a good deal of the time; he may even be over in the town drinking coffee. This is a possibility. But at the same time he is on the job working for the elevator company that has hired him and most farmers would know where to find him. He is going to say that he was on duty for eight or nine hours a day.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister would allow me to read section 109 of the Canada Grain Act. I think this is why there is a conflict here. It is not spelled out by the minister, and if he will spell it out we will accept what he says. Section 109 says:
Except as provided in section 108, the operator or manager-
It uses both terms:
-of every licensed public country elevator shall, at all reasonable hours on each day upon which the elevator is open, receive all grain offered thereat for storage without discrimination and in the order in which it is offered, provided that there

Canada Labour Code
is in the elevator available storage accommodation for grain of the variety and grade of such grain and of the character desired by the person by whom the grain is offered.
I think if this is spelled out, we would have no further argument.

It seems to me that there is no necessary contradiction between "reasonable hours" and the system provided in this clause, because presumably the grain act obligates the operator and manager to be available for reasonable hours. If the reasonable hours at a peak period are 12, we would make provision to take that into account in the average for the year. Surely in a slack period he is not obligated to be there for 12 hours; perhaps he is obligated to be there for eight hours, or perhaps only three hours. So you could average this out, and we believe it is a reasonable provision. We certainly would not think this would contradict the "reasonable hours" mentioned in the grain act. I think we are safe enough here.

I know that in the past elevator agents have been on duty in their elevators for 18 hours a day during certain periods, and others may not have to be there more than one or two hours on other days, but you cannot average it for a period of two or more weeks.
We can average up to 50 weeks in a year, if we need to. We can prescribe an average for two or more weeks in a year so that we have it-
So that you have it for the whole year?
Yes, so that we have it for the whole year, if need be.

In coming to an average would you expect the elevator operator to be there from, say, eight o'clock in the morning until noon and to be away for the rest of the afternoon? Is this what the minister means by averaging, that he can close up the elevator for half a day periodically to offset the hours he has worked for a longer period?

Presumably it is up to the management to decide the hours men shall work. From the facts the hon. member has mentioned, working four hours or three hours a day, we would average those days of few hours with the days having 10 or 12 hours of work over a period as long as is required to meet the needs of the par-

ticular operation. If the facts are as we have had them discussed, this looks after the situation.

This situation is going to be further agitated when rail line abandonment takes place-and I believe it is going to take place in certain areas-and farmers come in from many miles away with their grain and find the elevator closed. This is a situation against which we as legislators must guard, and protect our constituents. Although we are dealing with clause 5(2) here, it refers to clause 3(3), and I think before we conclude this matter we must have a definite statement from the minister that elevator operators or managers are not included. If my colleague is satisfied that it will be averaged over the year and he thinks this will look after the situation, or other members representing farm areas are satisfied this will be taken in the way the minister means it, and when the regulations come out they will not change the minister's meaning-which I have seen happen in other cases, where the regulations have been more powerful than the act itself-this would be sufficient; but I believe the minister should spell it out right now.

I have spelled it out as far as I can. I gather my explanation met with the approval of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Assiniboia; I thought they agreed with what I said in regard to the facts as we know them concerning variable hours. We certainly will utilize the provision to the limit, to meet the problem of the country elevators. I believe in this way we are going very far in that direction, and I do not believe hon. members would want us to go to the extent where the principles of the bill would be overcome.

Mr. Chairman, I merely want to get it completely clear in my mind. Supposing a farmer delivers a load of grain to the elevator and the elevator operator has been working really long hours for two or three weeks? A period of adjustment is provided to cut down the hours; if I understood the minister correctly he mentioned a figure of 2,000 hours. The elevator operator goes to his elevator at about eight o'clock in the morning-some go before that -and stays until six. In that case he will say he was on duty, and because of the fact he has worked there long hours he will say he is going to work just in the mornings for

two or three weeks and will close in the afternoons. That is not going to satisfy the farmer who comes in with a load of grain at four in the afternoon, only to find the elevator operator away, and rightly so because he has been averaging out his hours. I think this has to be spelled out in black and white so that everyone can understand it in no uncertain terms.
This legislation does not provide any authority for an employee to advance that argument. This is a matter he has to work out with his employer.

I do not want to get mixed up in the problems of country elevators but I would say that in the part of the country I come from, if that situation arose and an operation was required to be open 18 hours a day over a period of time, they would put on a second shift. That is one method of settling that kind of problem, it seems to me.
I rose, Mr. Chairman, because I am a little puzzled about what appears to me to be some conflict between clause 5, which is now under consideration, and clause 6. I want to know which one of these clauses is to be the operative clause as far as the bill is concerned when it becomes law. Clause 5 refers to standard hours of work and clause 6 refers to maximum hours of work. Clause 5 says that the hours of work shall not be longer than eight hours per day or 40 hours per week. In clause 6 it turns right around and says that an employer can require an employee to work 48 hours per week. Why is clause 6 there at all, particularly if one considers it in relation to the provisions of clause 9 which we will be coming to a little later on. The thing which concerns me is that some of the people who read this act when it becomes law are likely to decide that the present clause 6 is really the operative clause, and it may very well tend to become the standard provision rather than the exception. I think we should have some information on why clause 6 is there at all before we pass clause 5.

Clause 5, of course, establishes the standard day of eight hours and the standard week of 40 hours. The clause now mentioned allows for the working of 48 hours in a week, but the additional eight hours beyond the standard 40 must be at premium pay; in other words, at time and a half. That is set out in clause 8.
The hon. member referred to clauses 9 and 10 which provide for two instances where an employee may be required to work beyond 20220-584
Canada Labour Code
48 hours per week on the issuance of a permit by the minister. Second, there is a possibility that in the event of emergency conditions-for example, the breakdown of machinery or an accident occurring-work beyond the 48 hours may be required, in which case a report is subsequently made to the minister. So that actually a 40 hour work week is prescribed. Then there is the possibility of a 48 hour week at premium pay, and then work beyond a 48 hour week as a result of emergency conditions with a report made to the minister. That is the sequence.

If I might pursue the particular questioning I had in mind, the other matter which puzzles me is the relationship between subclause (2) of clause 5 and clause
7.	As I understand it, clause 7 imposes a limitation on the operation of subclause (2) of clause 5. I am not certain I am opposed to clause 7, but I am wondering how this averaging out principle will work under certain circumstances if it is limited by clause 7.
I have particularly in mind the kind of situation referred to earlier by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg in respect of employees in marine transportation and that sort of thing who may be out working for a period of time extending beyond seven days. I know there are some procedures which allow for people to be on duty for longer than seven days, with compensation provided under some union agreements for extra days off. I have in mind here ships returning to shore. But I am wondering whether the minister could explain what he understands to be the implications of clause 5(2) and its relationship to the operation of clause 7.

May I draw the hon. member's attention to the phrase "wherever practicable" in clause 7. Where it is impracticable of course to have a full day of rest on a Sunday, provision is made for one day of rest in the week. But it is to be on a Sunday wherever practicable. If work had to be done on a Sunday, presumably averaging would apply on that day as on any other.

Then may I ask the minister who decides when it is practicable? There are some areas in the bill where such matters may be defined by the regulations, but I have not noticed anywhere where this particular matter is set out in such a manner as to give the minister or the governor in council authority to make regulations defining what constitutes what is practicable or

Canada Labour Code
impracticable regarding Sunday as a normal day of rest.

I cannot tell my hon. friend at the moment who decides when it is practicable, but there is now an established law providing for this day of rest. Or, at least, it has a persuasive character and it is carried forward in this bill that Sunday shall be the normal day of rest in the week wherever practicable. If it is not practicable, then presumably another day of the week will be provided. The sanctions of the bill will presumably apply to this clause as to all others.

I think this is rather an important question because, if I may say so, sometimes this develops into a situation where the employer decides what is practicable. I can quote an example of this, which I admit falls outside the minister's jurisdiction.
Apparently the management of the British Columbia ferry authority has decided that their employees are going to work ten days on, straight through, and then so many days off. This has become quite a bone of contention and up until this time the employer, the B.C. ferry authority, has decided that the ten day period is to be worked by the employees. I would hate to see that kind of situation remain in respect of the operation of our national minimum standards, so that a group of employees is entirely at the mercy of an employer as far as the decision as to what is practicable is concerned. That is why I wonder whether the subject matter of clause 9 could more effectively be covered in some way by incorporating it in the provisions of subclause (2) of clause 5.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is agreed that there shall be provided one day a week off on a mandatory basis as a day of rest. That is an obligatory provision of this bill. Sunday is the normally accepted day of rest. There is no absolute assurance or sanction that Sunday will be the day off, but wherever practicable it shall be. It is presumably suggested that whenever Sunday is impracticable as the day of rest, clause 5 (2) shall apply. Certainly one could argue that this involves an irregular distribution of the man's hours of work when it is impracticable to have Sunday off.

Mr. Chairman, just before we pass clause 5, I should like to state that I have listened with interest to the discussion carried on by the hon. members for Swift Current and Assiniboia in

relation to grain elevators employees. It may be true that the hours worked by those employees can be averaged out for a period longer than two weeks, but I still envisage some complications in this regard.
In the event that an elevator operator operates his elevator on the prairies on an average of 12 hours a day in the fall for several months, then he would have to declare a similar period of months during the summer as a short work period-perhaps four hours per day-in order to strike an average. If I understand the wording of this bill correctly, this could greatly injure the grain handling trade, and I am thinking particularly of a year like last year when the grain handling companies did a tremendous job in respect of moving a large quantity of wheat for export.
I think the minister should make this averaging out principle a little more clear, because clause 3, as I read it, definitely includes the grain handling trade-the wheat board and grain elevator companies. The provision contained in clause 5 (2), embodying the averaging out technique for more than a two week period, does not really solve the problem to which I have referred. I think the provisions of this clause would eventually have the effect of increasing the cost of grain handling and make much more uneconomical the operation of some country elevators. Perhaps these provisions would bring about the abandonment of some country elevators, as well as some railway branch line abandonments. These abandonments would greatly contribute to the cost of grain handling, and I am sure no one in this house desires to see that happen in any of the grain producing areas of western Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I think this aspect of this bill should be given some further consideration. If the grain trade falls within the provisions of this act, there should be some further provision made, clearly setting out this averaging clause, so that an elevator may remain open only half a day during the wintertime in order to average out the working hours. It may be that that practice could only be followed by a certain portion of the total grain trading area, and I think a great deal of difficulty will be created by this provision for the Alberta wheat pool, the united grain growers and many other grain handling companies in western Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I should also like to draw the minister's attention to the fact that in many cases the farmers find themselves only able to deliver their quotas of grain to the

grain elevators in the last weeks of July, as a result of which further difficulty will be created in respect of the averaging out technique. I think there is a great deal of room for improvement in this portion of the bill. Perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce would give some consideration to this part of the bill, and perhaps between the two ministers a clear explanation can be worked out which would answer some of the questions asked in relation to the obvious complications which appear to exist. I should like the Minister of Labour to again clarify what is involved in this bill in relation to the grain trade.

Mr. Chairman, of course the principle of this bill is to provide for a 40 hour week. That principle was accepted on second reading. All employees under federal jurisdiction are to come within this provision. It has been argued and suggested that in the case of grain elevator companies, they would be obliged to pay an excessive amount of overtime during peak periods because of the nature of their operations. Clause 5(2) will permit these companies to average out the hours worked, even to the extent of a period of a full year, so that if an employee works on the average of 2,000 hours for 50 weeks, the employer would not be obliged to pay overtime until that employee had worked more than 2,000 hours. At that time, of course, he would be obliged to pay overtime, and that is the purpose of this bill. I think the provisions of this bill do clear up any difficulty which arises as a result of a seasonal operation. It may be that the elevator companies will occasionally have to pay overtime, and I am sure they do so now. It may well be that they will reorganize their operation, putting on an extra shift, or something of that nature. There are alternative ways of dealing with this seasonal type of operation. We think that in this bill we have met, to the maximum, any difficulty that arises from the seasonal nature of an operation.

Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock.
Progress reported.
