maintopic: AIR TRANSPORT-INQUIRY AS TO NEGOTIATIONS BETWEEN AIR CANADA AND C.P.A.
AIR TRANSPORT-INQUIRY AS TO NEGOTIATIONS BETWEEN AIR CANADA AND C.P.A.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I raised the other day and that I want to raise again tonight relates to the urgent need for the government to make some kind of statement on the negotiations that are going on between Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Airlines, particularly inasmuch as until some sort of conclusion has been reached the minister has told us he will not be in a position to even consider regional air carrier policy.
This question is not a new one. It is not even new to this session. If you look at the record of the first session of the twenty sixth parliament, you will see numerous occasions upon which members directed questions to the then minister of transport. From press reports we were led to believe that the former minister of transport, who is now the President of the Privy Council, was just on the verge of exploding with some kind of policy statement, when internal difficulties about regional carrier problems within the cabinet forced a change of duties. Consequently this matter was not raised again until February 26 of this year. The question is to be found on page 256 of Hansard, when the hon. member for Three Rivers asked the Minister of Transport when we could expect a statement. The last sentence of the minister's reply reads as follows:
I hope this will be before too long.
We all remember what happened on April 30, the night the minister attempted to make a policy statement over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and the resulting furore in the house. I do not intend to rehash that debacle. I should like to quote from the minister's statement the following day, which is found on page 2808 of Hansard:
I considered very carefully last Friday morning whether the very tentative decision which was taken by the government to carry on another stage in the formulation of air policy, which has not yet been formulated-

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
These are the pertinent words.
-and which I am sure will not be formulated for at least another month-
When the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines was examining the officials of Air Canada on June 22, the minister told us then, those of us who were on that committee, that he expected to make a statement around September 1. He asked us to forbear asking any further questions because this would only complicate negotiations that were then proceeding between Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Airlines. Well if you look at the record of this session, you will find members did refrain from asking any questions. Indeed the next time a question was asked on this subject was on September 3, two days after the time the minister thought he would be in a position to make a statement, at which time I asked a question. The minister's reply can be found on page 7613 of Hansard, as follows:
I can report that very active discussions have been going on between the two air lines since discussions commenced some months ago. I get progress reports from time to time, but X doubt that a statement at this stage would add very much to the prospects of success in these negotiations.
Again, Mr. Speaker, we were told not to ask questions because it could hamper prospects for success. Six weeks later, on October 13, I raised the question once more, and it was at that point Your Honour ruled the question was not one of urgency.
If you read the press you will have noticed that last Saturday the Ottawa Citizen carried a feature by Norman Campbell headed, "Parliament", in which he stated:
Meanwhile, parliament awaits the promised statement of government policy on Canadian air lines and the international routes...
More than six months ago, transport minister Pickersgill told the Commons the whole question of future air policy was under "very active consideration." He hoped it would not be too long until conclusions were reached and could be announced to the house.
Many Canadians see in this kind of hedging, this referral of a government decision basically to two air lines, Air Canada and C.P.A., a calculated manoeuvre not to get on with the problem of announcing a regional air carrier policy for the country. If he cannot make any statement tonight, may I appeal to the acting minister to try another television performance so that we may find out something about what is happening.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllraiih (Acting Minister of Transport):
maintopic: AIR TRANSPORT-INQUIRY AS TO NEGOTIATIONS BETWEEN AIR CANADA AND C.P.A.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the meeting which the Minister of Transport (Mr. 
Pickersgill) held with the presidents of the major railways and the presidents of Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Airlines to outline the basic principles which should apply in the development of Canadian aviation policy, a number of meetings have been held between working teams of the two air lines and between the two presidents of the air lines to discuss possible avenues of co-operation.
These discussions have not yet been completed and it would therefore be premature at this stage to attempt to make any detailed statement on the various items on which progress has been made. However, I am very happy to be able to state that the two air lines have jointly requested the following information to be made public, and I quote:
Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Air lines have agreed to co-operate in presenting a united Canadian effort in the highly competitive world of international air transportation.
The agreement follows a government request for greater co-operation between the two Canadian carriers.
Both carriers have agreed to "sell Canada first" by ensuring each adopts the other's service as first alternate to its own, consistent with customer requirements.
That is, if one carrier cannot accommodate a customer due to inconvenient routing or lack of space, it will book him on the other Canadian carrier before any foreign operator, providing it is not to the passenger's disadvantage.
Air Canada has also agreed to appoint C.P.A. as its general sales agent in many areas of the Orient, the South Pacific and South America, while C.P.A. will name Air Canada as its general sales agent in Bermuda, the Bahamas and the islands of the Caribbean.
Additional general sales agency appointments are under review.
The new policy is expected to improve service to passengers and shippers by providing greater Canadian representation in the areas concerned, while aiding both carriers in obtaining additional revenues on international services.

maintopic: TRANSPORTATION-PROPOSED REDUCTION IN C.P.R. SERVICE IN WESTERN CANADA
TRANSPORTATION-PROPOSED REDUCTION IN C.P.R. SERVICE IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday I raised the question of further curtailments in passenger train service between Calgary and Lethbridge, and between Lethbridge and Medicine Hat. Effective October 26 C.P.R. trains 307 and 308, now operating daily between Medicine Hat and Lethbridge, will be reduced to Monday, Wednesday and Friday from Lethbridge to Medicine Hat, and Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday from Medicine Hat to Lethbridge.
Trains 309 and 310 now operating Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday between Calgary and Lethbridge via Macleod subdivision will operate only on Wednesdays and Satur-

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
days. Trains 311 and 312 now operating Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Sunday between Calgary and Lethbridge via Alder-syde subdivision will operate only on Thursdays and Sundays.
The Railway Act does not require that a railway make application to the board of transport commissioners for authority to reduce passenger service. Such prior authorization by the board is required only where a passenger service is being completely discontinued. Accordingly, none of these reductions I have mentioned requires the board's approval. Under the Railway Act, however, the railways are obliged to maintain adequate service and facilities, and the board has full authority to require that reductions in passenger service, for example, be not proceeded with if in the board's opinion the reductions would reduce the service below what the board would consider adequate in the public interest. Furthermore, after the reduction has gone into effect, the board can order the restoration of the service for the same reasons.
The only notice given with respect to this reduction in rail service has been that posted in all the small railway stations between the points mentioned that service would be reduced within 30 days. Representations have been made to the Department of Transport, and I believe to the board of transport commissioners, that the service which would be left would not be adequate to meet the needs of the area I have mentioned. I think that in all fairness to the city of Lethbridge and the city of Medicine Hat, to the chambers of commerce in those cities and to other interested parties, there ought to be a longer period between the date when notice is given and the date when the reduction takes effect. My appeal to the minister tonight is that he request the board of transport commissioners to see that this period is extended by 60 days at least in order that the interested parties may have an opportunity to appear before the board and present their case. Then, if in the opinion of the commissioners the reduction is not likely to inflict an undue inconvenience on the communities concerned, the railways could proceed with the reduction in service which is contemplated. But up to the present time there has not been sufficient opportunity given.
I should like to say also that in my opinion during the last two months there has been a terrific upswing in demand for rail passenger service. I should like to quote from
an editorial which appeared in the Medicine
Hat News of September 26. It says this:
The entire railway situation is under review at the present. This would be a good time for the government, its board of transport commissioners and others concerned to probe the passenger service provided by the railways in this country.
Is the C.P.R., for example, deliberately attempting to discourage the public from travelling by rail?
Is the C.P.R., through this "policy" trying to steer would be train passengers to its air line?
The public has a right to know the answers to these and other questions inasmuch as public money subsidizes the railways.
Lastly, the politicians should ponder well the fact that there is a demand for rail service. Is it not to be met?
This involves much larger considerations than the local services I am talking about now, but I ask the minister tonight to take this into consideration, to get in touch with the board of transport commissioners and at least give the people concerned the opportunity to make representations.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (Acting Minister of Transport):
maintopic: TRANSPORTATION-PROPOSED REDUCTION IN C.P.R. SERVICE IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
I should like first of all to express my appreciation to the hon. member for the accuracy of his statement of the facts involved in his question, and for the accuracy of his statement of the law applicable. I might also add that he did me the courtesy of making his request in a wholly objective way.
The situation is that the board of transport commissioners has received complaints with respect to these changes and they are at present being considered. Since the changes in both of these services do not involve discontinuance of specific trains, but a reduction in the frequency of their operations, the board has taken no action to intervene on the strength of the representations which have been received from parties objecting to the changes.
In view of the volume of complaints received by the board, however, it has directed the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to file its submissions with respect to the specific points raised, and also to furnish the board with the particulars of the patronage of the existing services. It will be seen from what I have said that this matter is receiving the careful attention of the board.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-EGGS-REQUEST FOR CHANGE IN DEFICIENCY PAYMENT METHOD
AGRICULTURE-EGGS-REQUEST FOR CHANGE IN DEFICIENCY PAYMENT METHOD
speechtext:
I welcome this opportunity to debate a matter pertaining to the 2 cents deficiency payment to egg producers.
9220	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
As the house knows, these deficiency payments are based on the national weighted average price which farmers receive during a 12 months period. In my opinion this should have been on a regional, cumulative price basis. To justify my argument I should like to give hon. members this information. During the month of May on the prairies the price received for grade A large eggs was 17 cents. This included the cities of Edmonton, Calgary, Saskatoon, Swift Current, Regina, Melville, Brandon and Winnipeg. The price range was from 17 cents to 19 cents, while at the same time other places in the east received 35 cents. Victoria 32 cents, Vancouver and Kelowna 31 cents, Fort William, Toronto and other cities received 32 cents to 35 cents.
When the stabilization board establish the average price they take the low that the prairies received, normally 17 cents, and the high received by the egg producers in the east and on that basis they calculate what should be made as a deficiency payment. This year it is 2 cents. My argument is this. Instead of taking the national weighted average it should be done on the regional basis. The difference in price ranges from 17 cents to 35 cents. We on the prairies just help to get a higher price for these people who receive 35 cents and 37 cents; we lower the average. They will again receive 2 cents per dozen, while our fellows on the prairies who received 17 cents will also only receive 2 cents per dozen. My argument is that the price should be established on the regional basis instead of on the national basis.

Last year I had a resolution on the order paper to provide deficiency payments for eggs-and the same applies to hogs-on a cumulative regional price basis, rather than on a national weighted basis. Until this is done the egg producers in the west will never receive justice.

speakeroldname: Mr. B. S. Beer (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-EGGS-REQUEST FOR CHANGE IN DEFICIENCY PAYMENT METHOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for his question and for the opportunity of commenting on it briefly. I think the hon. member would agree that the purpose of deficiency payments under the price stabilization board is first of all to provide stability to the egg market, and second to provide a measure of guarantee to the small producer who may receive a deficiency payment on the first 4,000 dozen eggs that he produces.
I think the hon. member would also recognize that in view of the fact that this is a matter which might normally be regarded as government policy, he could not expect me to elaborate in too great detail. I do, however, wish to avail myself of the opportunity to comment briefly on this matter and say that the ideal situation of course would be where the production is nearly equal to the demand. Because production is difficult to regulate precisely, so may we expect price fluctuations. These fluctuations in production usually follow a pattern affected by the seasons of the year. To make deficiency payments on a quarterly basis, or even on a regional basis, would be to aggravate the situation and would tend to defeat the principle of price stabilization on a year round basis.
